virals.name: raph_guilhem
virals.text:
If you want to attract C-levels, VPs, or B2B decision-makers, create content around their specific pain points.

90% of your success is in the hook.

Here’s how I attracted 800+ comments and 50K impressions on LinkedIn yesterday, with decision-makers from major brands engaging.

1. Call out your ICP indirectly

“A marketing team from a $100M DTC brand…”

I’m not saying “Hey CMOs, read this.”

I’m mentioning a company size and industry that my target audience recognizes.

2. Trigger a pain they already have

“…showed me their complete BRAND BRAIN.”

Every marketing leader struggles with keeping their brand consistent across products, channels, creatives, and teams.

I’m showing something they wish they had.

3. Make the value tangible

Instead of writing “Here’s how to improve your brand strategy,” I show a visual breakdown of an actual Brand Brain.

The visual does the selling before anyone reads the post.

4. Create curiosity + FOMO

People see the framework but don’t have access to the full thing.

They immediately wonder what they’re missing.

5. Turn attention into qualified leads

“Comment BRAIN and I’ll send it over.”

Low-friction CTA. No landing page. No form, and send instantly with https://t.co/8prlaGC5oR 

And because the hook attracts the right people, the comments come from the right ICP.

Don’t create content about what your product does.

Create content around the problems your buyers desperately want to solve.

The best B2B content doesn’t just generate impressions. It attracts the people you want to sell to.

virals.name: ryangtanaka
virals.text:
I'm classically trained and come from a traditional arts background (been using my own music for our company's promo videos lately if you want to check them out) but I think a lot of the sentiment around the anti-AI camps have it all wrong - they should be welcoming the new cohorts of people identifying as "AI artists" with open arms. Here's why:

• Criticism from the public around your art is part of being an artist - which many of them are learning as we speak.

• For a lot of people - especially if they weren't privileged enough to have access to lessons when younger - AI is their "entry point" into learning the craft. The ones that want to take it to the next level will eventually get interested in learning the fundamentals (theory/form/composition/meaning/etc.) to improve their output.

• Both traditional and AI artists face the same problem: "how do I get paid for this?" There's a lot of things in the art/content spaces that needs fixing and this is an opportunity to get more people on the side of copyright/IP/royalties reform.

• As of now, AI-generated content is flooding all platforms everywhere, which will eventually cause the entire model to collapse - or, force companies to take the idea of quality control more seriously. (See above: the way to get quality is to actually pay the folks doing the work.)

• Recent AI models - as a combination of necessity and regulations - now are pretty good at giving attribution to its sources. This paves the way for royalties models that were not possible before.

I was always an AI-skeptic and still am - I get the frustrations behind the tech because early models were doing some blatantly illegal things, which has landed a lot of them in trouble now. But don't let that allow you to punch downwards or sideways - we don't need artists fighting other artists because that's exactly what they want. The battle isn't traditional artists vs AI artists, but artists vs. the law.

If you're going to get mad, do it with issues worth getting mad about - look up the Berne Convention and how it *doesn't* apply to creatives in the US, regardless of how the work was made. That's the stuff we should be focusing on if you really want things to change.

virals.name: Iamjaneezy
virals.text:
Can we talk about how DEMOTIVATING it is to create anything in 2026?

You write something intelligent.

“That’s ChatGPT.”

You build an app.

“AI built that.”

You make music.

“AI generated.”

You create a video.

“AI slop.”

You express an opinion.

“You’re a bot.”

I’m a software developer. I build with AI, and I know how much human effort still goes into making something actually work.

The failed attempts.

The debugging.

The sleepless nights.

The money spent.

The decisions AI cannot make for you.

But lately, it feels like the moment people hear AI was involved, they assume there was no skill, creativity or effort involved.

And sometimes, that genuinely makes me question whether I even want to share what I’m building.

I have so many things I want to create.

But I also wonder whether we’re entering an era where everyone can create, yet nobody respects creation anymore.

Have we become so obsessed with detecting AI that we’ve forgotten how to recognise human effort?

Creators, developers, writers, musicians, filmmakers…

Are you feeling this too?

Because I genuinely want to know.

meanwhile youtube gives partner creators 55% of ad revenue and says it paid out $100b+ to creators, artists and media companies in 4 years.

so now instagram is testing "features": videos up to 90 minutes.
plus "clips as reels", where short clips link back to the long video.

the lesson isn't "make long videos."

it's this:
short content gets attention.
long content gets trust.
only one of them pays the bills.

if your reels and posts don't lead somewhere deeper, you're renting attention you can't cash in.

outsiders.name: Iamjaneezy
outsiders.text:
Can we talk about how DEMOTIVATING it is to create anything in 2026?

You write something intelligent.

“That’s ChatGPT.”

You build an app.

“AI built that.”

You make music.

“AI generated.”

You create a video.

“AI slop.”

You express an opinion.

“You’re a bot.”

I’m a software developer. I build with AI, and I know how much human effort still goes into making something actually work.

The failed attempts.

The debugging.

The sleepless nights.

The money spent.

The decisions AI cannot make for you.

But lately, it feels like the moment people hear AI was involved, they assume there was no skill, creativity or effort involved.

And sometimes, that genuinely makes me question whether I even want to share what I’m building.

I have so many things I want to create.

But I also wonder whether we’re entering an era where everyone can create, yet nobody respects creation anymore.

Have we become so obsessed with detecting AI that we’ve forgotten how to recognise human effort?

Creators, developers, writers, musicians, filmmakers…

Are you feeling this too?

Because I genuinely want to know.

drafts.draft_en:
Most creative stress isn't from the work.

It's from the things you're avoiding.

The price you haven't named.
The post you haven't shared.
The client you haven't called.

Do the uncomfortable thing sooner.
The making gets lighter.
drafts.video_tip: 20s talking head in your studio. One cut per avoided thing, each word popping up as a caption. End with you hitting 'post' on your phone, close-up.

drafts.draft_en:
You don't need more talent to sell your work.

You need more self-belief.

Skills you can learn in a weekend.
Believing it's worth paying for takes daily practice.
drafts.video_tip: Hands-only shot of you making something, voiceover line by line. Last line on a black frame, large text.

drafts.draft_en:
Everyone says AI will flood the world with content.

Fine.

It can't sit six strangers around a table and make them friends by dessert.

Host the room.
That's the work now.
drafts.video_tip: Timelapse of a table set for six, then candles lit and people sitting down. Text overlay for each line. Natural room sound, no music.

drafts.draft_en:
It's almost impossible to beat a creative who is having fun.

They ship more.
They quit less.
They sell without sounding desperate.

If the work feels like a chore, fix that before you fix your marketing.
drafts.video_tip: Selfie mid-session, laughing at a mistake, then show the finished piece. One take, captions burned in.
